options.label: TypeScript + Vite web app under dev/console/

questions.question: What should the dev console be built in?

options.description: The console is a different product with a different audience; its own numbered spec and its own gallery keep the app's spec about the app. Costs a second coverage gate and runner (copied from the existing one), and I'd confirm the executable-requirements pack tolerates two suites in one repo.
options.label: Its own suite, dev/console/requirements/ (Recommended)

options.description: One spec, one gate, one gallery, no duplicated runner machinery. But the app's requirements document — the thing you review to approve the product — grows a large section about an internal tool, and the test package gains a dependency on the console package.
options.label: New sections in the existing dev/requirements/requirements.md

questions.question: Where do the dev console's executable requirements live?

options.description: You open a URL, no toolchain. Adds Hosting to firebase.json and one console step to the front-loaded human checklist (enable Hosting), and a chain link that deploys it. Anyone with the URL can drive the 4 sim accounts — dev project only, so acceptable.
options.label: Deploy to Firebase Hosting on the dev project (Recommended)

options.description: No hosting setup, nothing exposed. You need a Flutter toolchain and a checkout to validate, and I can't screenshot it from this container (no Chrome here), so the goldens in the spec would be the only thing I can show you before you run it yourself.
options.label: Run it locally (flutter run -d chrome)

questions.question: How do you want to look at the console when it's time to validate it? (This is the gate that unblocks the Appetize chain.)

options.description: A 30-minute scripted walk-and-send plan replays in 30 seconds against the real dev backend, with presence heartbeats rewritten at the accelerated cadence. Everything real, everything fast — except scenarios that need presence to go STALE, which must run at real time (a '5 minutes of silence' step the console waits out honestly).
options.label: Compress the plan against the real clock (Recommended)

options.description: The above, plus a second mode running the console against the Firebase emulator suite where I can drive time-sensitive scenarios differently. More machinery, and the emulator is not the real backend — a green emulator run proves less than a real one.
options.label: Compress, and add an emulator mode for staleness

questions.question: What should "speeding up time" actually mean? The backend's 5-minute presence freshness is judged server-side against Firestore's own serverTimestamp, so no client can make the real server's clock move faster.

answers.How do you want to look at the console w: Deploy to Firebase Hosting on the dev project (Recommended)
answers.What should \"speeding up time\" actuall: Compress with emulator mode (for a varaiety of reasons, not to mention reality-sanity-checks that people aren't "walking" at 600 kmph and sending 20 messages a second). This will actually allow us to verify more in the long run. Make sure that any "emulator mode" data that is send in dev mode to allow our manipulations is (obviously) not read in the prod version, but also validate that it is not send from the client in prod mode, and validate it is purged from the requests at the edge, if it did arrive. This is on top of making sure the server code is correctly not reading emulator mode in prod.

# /do-later — defer a change into a chained request run

File the deferred change as an **ad-hoc request** (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §16): an issue the
queue picks up on its own, held behind what is still in flight — never an ordinary issue,
which waits for somebody to remember it.

You are filing work, not doing it. Touch no source file, open no branch.

## What you write

**One issue, well defined.** The run that implements it will never see this
conversation — the issue body is the whole brief. State the change, the files or
surfaces it touches if you know them, what "done" looks like, and anything the
owner ruled out. Size it to its idea; a rename is a sentence.

**Every field a run reads is one block on the first lines of the description**,
above the marker and ahead of your prose — the waits and the parameters together,
verbatim in this spelling:

```
Blocked-by: #<what this waits on>
Not-before: <ISO instant this may first run>
Model: <opus | sonnet | haiku>
```

### The coded form — for a URL-readable artifact

```
Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
Task: claudinite-tasks/verify-production
Live-probe: <url> :: <assertion that becomes true when the release lands>
Verify-probe: <url> :: <the assertion being verified>
Retry-every: <how often to re-probe while not yet live, e.g. 6 hours>
```

The probes are the whole check, executed in code by the task the `Task:` line names —
no session, no `Model:`. `Live-probe:` is `In-production-when:` made executable and
`Verify-probe:` is `Verify:`; both classes are required, repeat either line for more

---
name: writing-handover-issues
description: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
metadata:
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'mcp__github__issue_write.body /- \[ \]/'
---

# Writing a task for a human

An issue you will act on is a *description*. An issue a **person** will act on is an
*instrument*: they open it with the settings page in the next tab, and every word that is
not the next click is in the way. The two are written differently, and the second one is
almost always written like the first.

The failure is not being wrong. It is being **complete** — the reader skims, loses the
thread, and does three of six steps.

## The body has exactly two parts, in this order

1. **The checklist.** Checkboxes and nothing else. No prose between them, no italic
   asides under them, no notes about what breaks. A reader must be able to work top to
   bottom without their eye leaving the boxes.
2. **Everything else, below it.** Why the task exists, what each step buys, what stays
   broken while it is undone, background, links to the design. All of it, after the
   last checkbox, under its own heading.

One or two sentences may sit *above* the checklist to say what the issue is for. Not
more. If you find yourself explaining a step, you are writing part 2 — move it down.

Splitting them is the whole skill. The information the corpus asks a handover to carry
— what breaks while each step is off — still has to be there; it just has to be
somewhere the person executing is not reading.

## One step, one line, one action

A checkbox is an **imperative** naming one thing to do:

> - [ ] Set the repository variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` → [Variables](https://github.com/o/r/settings/variables/actions)

Not `You will need to set…`, not a step that also explains, not a step that is really
two. If a step needs a second sentence, either it is two steps or that sentence is
background. If it needs a paragraph, it is a sub-issue.

Bold nothing inside a step. Emphasis on every line is emphasis on none, and these lines
are already the only thing in their section.

## Link the screen, don't describe the path

Every step that happens in a UI carries **the deepest URL that lands on that screen**,
as the step's own link. Never a breadcrumb trail — `Settings → Secrets and variables →
Actions → Variables` is four things to get right and a link is zero.

Substitute the real owner and repo into the URL; a template with `<owner>` in it is a
breadcrumb wearing a link's clothes. Open every link, or construct it from a page you
have actually seen — a settings URL that 404s costs more than the trail you replaced.

## Getting a value: say where on the screen it is

The step that *produces* a value is the one that goes wrong, because the writer knows
the page and the reader does not. Name, in the words that appear on that screen:

- the control that mints or reveals it — *"press Generate a new client secret"*
- where the value then appears — *"the value shown once, under Client secrets"*
- what it looks like, when that disambiguates — *"begins `Iv23`"*, *"a 32-character hex
  string"*
- if it is shown once, say so **in that step**. That is not an explanation; it is part
  of the action.

> - [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — [App settings](https://github.com/settings/apps/x), top of the page under the app name

A value produced by one step and consumed by another is named identically in both, so
the reader can find what to paste.

## Order so that every step is doable when it is reached

Walk the list as the reader: at each box, does everything it needs already exist? A step
asking for a value a later step mints is the most common defect, and it reads perfectly
to the author.

Then close the gaps. A step that **mints or reveals a value** and the step that
**pastes it where it lives** are one pair, and they go immediately after each other —
never a block of producers followed later by a block of consumers, however tidily each
block groups by screen. Every box between them is a value the reader is holding in
their head while doing something else, and one that is shown once is held there at the
price of minting it again. Pair by pair beats phase by phase even when it means opening
the same screen twice.

That pairing is what keeps the value out of the reader's head, so it is also the reason
the list needs no note reminding them to hold it.

## Drop the steps that are not steps

A box that is usually a no-op teaches the reader to skim exactly the list that exists to
stop them skimming. If the honest answer for most readers is "nothing to do", it is
background, or it is a decision stated once above the list — not a checkbox.

## Close with one observable

End the issue with the single thing the person can look at to know they are done, in
what they will see rather than what will be true. Not "sign-in works" — *"loading the
page signed out shows Sign in with GitHub, and clicking it returns you signed in"*.

## Before you file

- Read only the checkboxes, in order. Can a person who has never seen this repo do
  them? That is the artifact; everything else is the appendix.
- Count the words in the longest box. If it is over about fifteen, it is carrying an
  explanation.
- Confirm each link resolves and each named control still has that name.

## Where this applies

Any issue whose body asks a person to click, set, register, install or copy: the
human-only handover basics requires, a pack's `adoptionHandover` rendered into an issue,
a migration's out-of-band setup phase, a production verification someone else will run.
The rule that such work gets **its own issue** rather than a note in a PR body is
basics' *Handing over a step only a human can perform*; this is how that issue is
written.

---
name: production-retrospective
description: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
---

# Production retrospective

[verify-in-production](../verify-in-production/SKILL.md) proves a **point assertion**, once:
artifact X reads Y, pass or fail. An element big enough to have a design deserves a second look of
a different kind — not "did it go live" but "did the design survive contact". Once it has worked
*as planned* for about a week, somebody should read its production record and answer four
questions:

1. **Is it working?** Every part of its loop ran and closed — count the strands, the wrong
   closes, the parks, not just the happy paths.
2. **Is it misused?** Do people or neighbouring machinery interact with it against its contract?
3. **Is it overused?** Which uses cost runs or attention and returned nothing — and what should
   the bar exclude?
4. **Is it underused?** What did the design mean to cover that nothing reaches — a trigger that
   never fires, a manual ask that should have been a mechanism?

The four questions are only the frame. What gives them teeth is a brief that already knows what
the element was *supposed* to do — and that knowledge exists exactly once, while the element is
being designed. So this skill has two moments: the brief is **written with the design**, and the
review **runs** a week into production. The reader at either moment must not be the author's
memory: the review is filed as a mechanism that comes back on its own (RULES.md's *When verifying
now is genuinely impossible* names the principle; this skill is its review-shaped sibling).

## When one is owed

The bar: **the element earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue.** A minor feature files no
retrospective — its proof is a test that ran, or verify-in-production's point assertion, and this
skill adds nothing to that. Filing retrospectives for small changes buries the reviews that matter
under reviews with nothing to find.

Two triggers own the filing today:

- **A migration plan's chain.** The retrospective is the chain's **last link**, filed with the
  rest of the chain when the plan is agreed —
  [writing-migration-plans](../writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md) owns the chain's mechanics. It
  rides `Blocked-by:` on the final execution step, so the queue holds it until the migration is
  actually done.
- **A merge that completes a design-doc'd element outside any chain.** File it at the merge,
  beside verify-in-production's own filing moment — the two are separate calls, and a point
  assertion neither requires nor replaces the retrospective.

## The brief is written at design time, not when the retrospective runs

What to retrospect on is a design question, answered while the element is being designed — in the
same pass that writes the design doc, and recorded in the retrospective issue's body (with the
expectations themselves in the design doc, where they are part of the end state). Answered when
the retrospective runs it is too late twice over: the designer's intent has left everyone's head,
and a number nobody thought to record cannot be read back. The brief answers, concretely, for
*this* element:

- **What is expected to happen, and in what amounts.** Volumes and rates, not adjectives: how
  many filings, runs, adoptions, visits per week; which counts should be zero and which would be
  worrying at zero. An expectation without a quantity cannot be missed.
- **What behaviours are expected** — from users and from neighbouring machinery. Who reaches for
  it, when, instead of what; what they were doing before it existed.

name: production-retrospective
description: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
---

# Production retrospective

[verify-in-production](../verify-in-production/SKILL.md) proves a **point assertion**, once:
artifact X reads Y, pass or fail. An element big enough to have a design deserves a second look of
a different kind — not "did it go live" but "did the design survive contact". Once it has worked
*as planned* for about a week, somebody should read its production record and answer four
questions:

1. **Is it working?** Every part of its loop ran and closed — count the strands, the wrong
   closes, the parks, not just the happy paths.
2. **Is it misused?** Do people or neighbouring machinery interact with it against its contract?
3. **Is it overused?** Which uses cost runs or attention and returned nothing — and what should
   the bar exclude?
4. **Is it underused?** What did the design mean to cover that nothing reaches — a trigger that
   never fires, a manual ask that should have been a mechanism?

The four questions are only the frame. What gives them teeth is a brief that already knows what
the element was *supposed* to do — and that knowledge exists exactly once, while the element is
being designed. So this skill has two moments: the brief is **written with the design**, and the
review **runs** a week into production. The reader at either moment must not be the author's
memory: the review is filed as a mechanism that comes back on its own (RULES.md's *When verifying
now is genuinely impossible* names the principle; this skill is its review-shaped sibling).

## When one is owed

The bar: **the element earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue.** A minor feature files no
retrospective — its proof is a test that ran, or verify-in-production's point assertion, and this
skill adds nothing to that. Filing retrospectives for small changes buries the reviews that matter
under reviews with nothing to find.

Two triggers own the filing today:

- **A migration plan's chain.** The retrospective is the chain's **last link**, filed with the
  rest of the chain when the plan is agreed —
  [writing-migration-plans](../writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md) owns the chain's mechanics. It
  rides `Blocked-by:` on the final execution step, so the queue holds it until the migration is
  actually done.
- **A merge that completes a design-doc'd element outside any chain.** File it at the merge,
  beside verify-in-production's own filing moment — the two are separate calls, and a point
  assertion neither requires nor replaces the retrospective.

## The brief is written at design time, not when the retrospective runs

What to retrospect on is a design question, answered while the element is being designed — in the
same pass that writes the design doc, and recorded in the retrospective issue's body (with the
expectations themselves in the design doc, where they are part of the end state). Answered when
the retrospective runs it is too late twice over: the designer's intent has left everyone's head,
and a number nobody thought to record cannot be read back. The brief answers, concretely, for
*this* element:

- **What is expected to happen, and in what amounts.** Volumes and rates, not adjectives: how
  many filings, runs, adoptions, visits per week; which counts should be zero and which would be
  worrying at zero. An expectation without a quantity cannot be missed.
- **What behaviours are expected** — from users and from neighbouring machinery. Who reaches for
  it, when, instead of what; what they were doing before it existed.

# The dev console — scripted actors against the real backend

The app's executable requirements ([dev/requirements/](../dev/requirements/requirements.md))
prove every screen and gesture against scripted fakes: no phone, no server, no
network. Nothing in this repository exercises the other half — that a real client,
holding a real token, writing real presence, gets the delivery
[DESIGN.md §4](DESIGN.md) describes. Hyperlocal delivery cannot be observed with one
client: the whole product is *who else was near you*, and a single device is always
alone in its cell.

The dev console is that second half. It is a second client of the same backend, driving
four simulated accounts along planned paths, sending planned messages, and showing what
each of the four actually received.

## What it is

A Flutter web app at `dev/console/`, deployed to Firebase Hosting on the dev project. It
is a development instrument, not part of the product: it ships in no store, it is never
pointed at production, and the app under `app/` neither imports it nor knows it exists.

It is Flutter for one reason that outweighs the rest: it reuses this repository's
committed geohash encoder (`app/lib/geo/geohash.dart`) and message models by path
dependency rather than transcribing them a third time. A TypeScript console would add a
third copy of the encoding contract the
[shouts-and-whispers pack](../.claudinite/local/packs/shouts-and-whispers/RULES.md)
already spends two checks guarding, and would need a parallel requirements harness built
from nothing.

## The four actors

Four email/password accounts on the dev project, signed in simultaneously through four
named `FirebaseApp` instances so each holds its own auth state, its own Firestore client
and its own feed subscription. The backend sees four ordinary users; nothing about a sim
actor is privileged, and the console holds no admin credential.

Four, rather than a number, because four is what the interesting cases need: a sender, a
recipient inside the whisper radius, a recipient inside the shout radius but outside the
whisper's, and one who is out of range or stale. Every delivery rule in
[DESIGN.md §1](DESIGN.md) is expressible with those four seats.

## The plan

A plan is the console's document, and it is pure data — editable, replayable, and
shareable as JSON:

- **A path per actor**: waypoints on the map with a time offset each. Between two
  waypoints the actor moves at whatever speed the pair implies; the editor rejects a pair
  implying a speed no person walks.
- **Sends pinned along the path**: an offset, a kind (shout or whisper), and the text.
  The send happens wherever the actor is at that offset, and the console draws the
  message's origin and its radius on the map.
- **A duration** the plan runs for.

The editor is the product surface: place a path, place a send, press play, watch the four
feeds fill.

## Two run modes, and why the fast one cannot use the real backend

| | real-time | compressed |
|---|---|---|
| speed | 1× | any multiplier |
| backend | the dev project | the Firebase emulator suite |
| clock | Firestore `serverTimestamp()` | a virtual clock the console supplies |
| what it proves | the real fan-out, rules and callable work end to end | the delivery rules hold across time-dependent scenarios |

Compressed replay cannot run against a real backend, and not merely because
`PRESENCE_TTL_MS` is judged server-side against a clock no client can move. A plan
replayed at 60× *is* an actor walking at 600 km/h and sending twenty messages a second.
Those are exactly the shapes a real backend should learn to refuse — implausible speed and
implausible rate are anti-spoofing signals the product does not have yet
([DESIGN.md §7](DESIGN.md)) and will want. Teaching the dev backend to tolerate them
would spend the one environment where such a rule could be developed. So compression runs
against the emulator, where a virtual clock is honest, and the dev project only ever sees
plausible traffic.

Real-time mode against the dev project is what proves the backend works. Compressed mode
against the emulator is what makes time-dependent scenarios — presence going stale, a
cooldown expiring, a message that arrives one second too late — cheap enough to keep as
regression cases.

## Sim time: the wire contract

In compressed mode the console supplies the instant itself. Two fields carry it, both
namespaced under a single `sim` object so one predicate finds them:

- on the `sendMessage` call: `sim.now` — the virtual instant the send happens at;
- on a presence write: `sim.updatedAt` — the virtual instant the heartbeat was reported
  at, standing in for `serverTimestamp()`.

There is no third field and no bare top-level spelling. One object, one predicate, one
thing to strip.

## Why sim fields cannot reach production

A field that lets a client dictate the server's notion of *now* is the strongest
capability in this system: it defeats the cooldown, it revives stale presence, and it
backdates delivery. It exists because the emulator needs it, and four independent guards
keep it there. Each is meant to hold alone.

1. **The server admits it only under the emulator.** The gate is a runtime signal a
   deployed function cannot carry (`FUNCTIONS_EMULATOR`, which the Functions emulator sets
   and a deploy never does) — read once at module load into a single exported constant, and
   never re-derived from anything in a request. A request cannot argue its way past it,
   because nothing in the request is consulted.
2. **The edge strips it.** Outside the emulator the callable deletes the `sim` object from
   the request before a single line of handler logic reads it, and logs that it did. The
   handler is therefore written against a request shape where the field cannot exist, and
   the log is what makes a stripped request distinguishable from one that never carried the
   field — a swallowed strip is a silent capability, which is what
   [basics](../.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/RULES.md) means by code that can silently do
   nothing.
3. **Firestore rules reject it.** Presence writes carrying a client-set `updatedAt` are
   refused by the ruleset, so the capability is closed at the boundary the functions do not
   sit in front of.
4. **No product client can send it.** The app under `app/` has no code that writes a `sim`
   field, and a committed check keeps it that way — the console is the only client that
   knows the spelling.

Guards 1 and 2 are the server's; 3 is the boundary's; 4 is the client's. The
[spec-driven-product](../.claudinite/shared/packs/spec-driven-product/RULES.md) rule that
a requirement is proved at every tier that enforces it applies exactly here: this is one
requirement with four proofs, not one proof reused.

## What the console observes

Per actor: its live feed, its presence doc's freshness, and its position on the map. Per
send: the origin, the radius circle, the `recipientCount` the callable returned, and which
of the four actually received it — the matrix that makes a delivery bug visible rather
than inferable. A send whose reported count and observed recipients disagree is the
console's headline finding, because that disagreement is the one bug the app itself can
never show you.

## Its executable requirements

`dev/console/requirements/` — its own numbered spec, its own coverage gate, its own
gallery, in the shape [dev/requirements/](../dev/requirements/README.md) established. A
separate suite rather than new sections in the app's: the app's requirements document is
what the owner reads to approve *the product*, and an internal instrument's screens do not
belong in that review.

The console's own cases run against fakes like any other suite. That its real replay works
against a real backend is not something a golden can hold, and the console is itself the
instrument for observing it.

input.body:
Tracking issue for two initiatives run as one chain: a **dev console** that drives four
simulated accounts against the real backend, and — gated on a human validation of that
console — the **Appetize preview** of the Android app (#99).

The end state of the console, and why it is shaped this way, is
[docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md](https://github.com/missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers/blob/main/docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md).
This issue holds the plan; it is append-only while the work runs.

## Why the console comes first

Nothing in this repository has ever observed the backend working. `app/`'s 21 tests and
`dev/requirements/`'s 70 cases all run against scripted fakes; the functions' 14 tests are
pure-logic. Hyperlocal delivery cannot be observed with one client — the product *is* who
else was near you — so the first real proof of the backend needs several clients at once.
That instrument is worth more than a demo link, and the demo link is better once it exists.

## Decisions taken (2026-09-06)

| decision | choice |
|---|---|
| demo/console backend | reuse `shouts-whispers-dev` |
| preview sign-in | email/password demo account (the app has only Google Sign-In today) |
| seeding | scripted sim actors from the console, not a static seeder |
| console stack | Flutter web, `dev/console/` |
| console spec | its own suite, `dev/console/requirements/` |
| console access | Firebase Hosting on the dev project |
| time control | real-time against dev; compressed against the emulator |
| Android app id | keep `com.shoutsandwhispers.shouts_and_whispers` |

## The plan

**Phase 0 — out-of-band setup (human, front-loaded).** Everything needing a console, an
account or a secret, before any code depends on it.

- [ ] #TBD_HANDOVER — Firebase console steps, sim accounts, Hosting, and the repository secrets

**Phase 1 — the stack (all written, one approval, merged as a chain).**

- [ ] #TBD_DESIGN — the design doc (this plan's own PR)
- [ ] #TBD_SIMTIME — sim-time wire contract and its four guards, server + rules + checks
- [ ] #TBD_SHELL — console package, plan model, plan editor, and its requirements suite
- [ ] #TBD_REPLAY — replay engine and observation views, real-time against dev
- [ ] #TBD_COMPRESSED — compressed mode against the emulator suite
- [ ] #TBD_HOSTING — Hosting config and the deploy path

**Phase 2 — execution (the chain runs itself).**

- [ ] #TBD_DEPLOY — deploy the console and post its URL
- [ ] #TBD_GATE — **human validation gate**: the owner drives the console and confirms it. Nothing below starts until this closes.

**Phase 3 — the Appetize preview (#99), released by the gate.**

- [ ] #TBD_EMAILAUTH — email/password sign-in path in the app, with its requirement leaf
- [ ] #TBD_ANDROID — Firebase config wiring, the google-services Gradle plugin, and the APK build task
- [ ] #TBD_UPLOAD — upload to Appetize, capture the public URL, document it
- [ ] #TBD_VERIFY — verify the preview is live and interactive
- [ ] #TBD_RETRO — retrospective, once both have lived a week

## Expected human gates

Two, and they are deliberate: the phase-0 checklist, and the validation gate. Every other
link carries an automerge policy predicting its own folder, so a park anywhere else means a
change reached further than this plan predicted — which is the speed bump working, not an
error to route around.

## What was measured before planning (2026-09-06)

- `cd app && flutter test` — 21 passed
- `cd dev/requirements && python3 run_requirements.py` — 70 passed
- `cd firebase/functions && npm run build && npm test` — clean, 14 passed
- `node --test .claudinite/local/packs/shouts-and-whispers/pack.test.mjs` — 24 passed
- Whether `shouts-whispers-dev` exists and is deployed: **unverified**. Firestore's REST
  API answers `403 CONSUMER_INVALID` identically for a project that does not exist, and
  `cloudfunctions.net` is egress-blocked from the session that planned this. Phase 0's
  first checkbox settles it.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/ShoutsAndWhispers/.claude/skills/writing-handover-issues

# Writing a task for a human

An issue you will act on is a *description*. An issue a **person** will act on is an
*instrument*: they open it with the settings page in the next tab, and every word that is
not the next click is in the way. The two are written differently, and the second one is
almost always written like the first.

The failure is not being wrong. It is being **complete** — the reader skims, loses the
thread, and does three of six steps.

## The body has exactly two parts, in this order

1. **The checklist.** Checkboxes and nothing else. No prose between them, no italic
   asides under them, no notes about what breaks. A reader must be able to work top to
   bottom without their eye leaving the boxes.
2. **Everything else, below it.** Why the task exists, what each step buys, what stays
   broken while it is undone, background, links to the design. All of it, after the
   last checkbox, under its own heading.

One or two sentences may sit *above* the checklist to say what the issue is for. Not
more. If you find yourself explaining a step, you are writing part 2 — move it down.

Splitting them is the whole skill. The information the corpus asks a handover to carry
— what breaks while each step is off — still has to be there; it just has to be
somewhere the person executing is not reading.

## One step, one line, one action

A checkbox is an **imperative** naming one thing to do:

> - [ ] Set the repository variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` → [Variables](https://github.com/o/r/settings/variables/actions)

Not `You will need to set…`, not a step that also explains, not a step that is really
two. If a step needs a second sentence, either it is two steps or that sentence is
background. If it needs a paragraph, it is a sub-issue.

Bold nothing inside a step. Emphasis on every line is emphasis on none, and these lines
are already the only thing in their section.

## Link the screen, don't describe the path

Every step that happens in a UI carries **the deepest URL that lands on that screen**,
as the step's own link. Never a breadcrumb trail — `Settings → Secrets and variables →
Actions → Variables` is four things to get right and a link is zero.

Substitute the real owner and repo into the URL; a template with `<owner>` in it is a
breadcrumb wearing a link's clothes. Open every link, or construct it from a page you
have actually seen — a settings URL that 404s costs more than the trail you replaced.

## Getting a value: say where on the screen it is

The step that *produces* a value is the one that goes wrong, because the writer knows
the page and the reader does not. Name, in the words that appear on that screen:

- the control that mints or reveals it — *"press Generate a new client secret"*
- where the value then appears — *"the value shown once, under Client secrets"*
- what it looks like, when that disambiguates — *"begins `Iv23`"*, *"a 32-character hex
  string"*
- if it is shown once, say so **in that step**. That is not an explanation; it is part
  of the action.

> - [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — [App settings](https://github.com/settings/apps/x), top of the page under the app name

A value produced by one step and consumed by another is named identically in both, so
the reader can find what to paste.

## Order so that every step is doable when it is reached

Walk the list as the reader: at each box, does everything it needs already exist? A step
asking for a value a later step mints is the most common defect, and it reads perfectly
to the author.

Then close the gaps. A step that **mints or reveals a value** and the step that
**pastes it where it lives** are one pair, and they go immediately after each other —
never a block of producers followed later by a block of consumers, however tidily each
block groups by screen. Every box between them is a value the reader is holding in
their head while doing something else, and one that is shown once is held there at the
price of minting it again. Pair by pair beats phase by phase even when it means opening
the same screen twice.

That pairing is what keeps the value out of the reader's head, so it is also the reason
the list needs no note reminding them to hold it.

## Drop the steps that are not steps

A box that is usually a no-op teaches the reader to skim exactly the list that exists to
stop them skimming. If the honest answer for most readers is "nothing to do", it is
background, or it is a decision stated once above the list — not a checkbox.

## Close with one observable

End the issue with the single thing the person can look at to know they are done, in
what they will see rather than what will be true. Not "sign-in works" — *"loading the
page signed out shows Sign in with GitHub, and clicking it returns you signed in"*.

## Before you file

- Read only the checkboxes, in order. Can a person who has never seen this repo do
  them? That is the artifact; everything else is the appendix.
- Count the words in the longest box. If it is over about fifteen, it is carrying an
  explanation.
- Confirm each link resolves and each named control still has that name.

## Where this applies

Any issue whose body asks a person to click, set, register, install or copy: the
human-only handover basics requires, a pack's `adoptionHandover` rendered into an issue,
a migration's out-of-band setup phase, a production verification someone else will run.
The rule that such work gets **its own issue** rather than a note in a PR body is
basics' *Handing over a step only a human can perform*; this is how that issue is
written.

1	# The dev console — scripted actors against the real backend
2	
3	The app's executable requirements ([dev/requirements/](../dev/requirements/requirements.md))
4	prove every screen and gesture against scripted fakes: no phone, no server, no
5	network. Nothing in this repository exercises the other half — that a real client,
6	holding a real token, writing real presence, gets the delivery
7	[DESIGN.md §4](DESIGN.md) describes. Hyperlocal delivery cannot be observed with one
8	client: the whole product is *who else was near you*, and a single device is always
9	alone in its cell.
10	
11	The dev console is that second half. It is a second client of the same backend, driving
12	four simulated accounts along planned paths, sending planned messages, and showing what
13	each of the four actually received.
14	
15	## What it is
16	
17	A Flutter web app at `dev/console/`, deployed to Firebase Hosting on the dev project. It
18	is a development instrument, not part of the product: it ships in no store, it is never
19	pointed at production, and the app under `app/` neither imports it nor knows it exists.
20	
21	It is Flutter for one reason that outweighs the rest: it reuses this repository's
22	committed geohash encoder (`app/lib/geo/geohash.dart`) and message models by path
23	dependency rather than transcribing them a third time. A TypeScript console would add a
24	third copy of the encoding contract the
25	[shouts-and-whispers pack](../.claudinite/local/packs/shouts-and-whispers/RULES.md)
26	already spends two checks guarding, and would need a parallel requirements harness built
27	from nothing.
28	
29	## The four actors
30	
31	Four email/password accounts on the dev project, signed in simultaneously through four
32	named `FirebaseApp` instances so each holds its own auth state, its own Firestore client
33	and its own feed subscription. The backend sees four ordinary users; nothing about a sim
34	actor is privileged, and the console holds no admin credential.
35	
36	Four, rather than a number, because four is what the interesting cases need: a sender, a
37	recipient inside the whisper radius, a recipient inside the shout radius but outside the
38	whisper's, and one who is out of range or stale. Every delivery rule in
39	[DESIGN.md §1](DESIGN.md) is expressible with those four seats.
40	
41	## The plan
42	
43	A plan is the console's document, and it is pure data — editable, replayable, and
44	shareable as JSON:
45	
46	- **A path per actor**: waypoints on the map with a time offset each. Between two
47	  waypoints the actor moves at whatever speed the pair implies; the editor rejects a pair
48	  implying a speed no person walks.
49	- **Sends pinned along the path**: an offset, a kind (shout or whisper), and the text.
50	  The send happens wherever the actor is at that offset, and the console draws the
51	  message's origin and its radius on the map.
52	- **A duration** the plan runs for.
53	
54	The editor is the product surface: place a path, place a send, press play, watch the four
55	feeds fill.
56	
57	## Two run modes, and why the fast one cannot use the real backend
58	
59	| | real-time | compressed |
60	|---|---|---|
61	| speed | 1× | any multiplier |
62	| backend | the dev project | the Firebase emulator suite |
63	| clock | Firestore `serverTimestamp()` | a virtual clock the console supplies |
64	| what it proves | the real fan-out, rules and callable work end to end | the delivery rules hold across time-dependent scenarios |
65	
66	Compressed replay cannot run against a real backend, and not merely because
67	`PRESENCE_TTL_MS` is judged server-side against a clock no client can move. A plan
68	replayed at 60× *is* an actor walking at 600 km/h and sending twenty messages a second.
69	Those are exactly the shapes a real backend should learn to refuse — implausible speed and
70	implausible rate are anti-spoofing signals the product does not have yet
71	([DESIGN.md §7](DESIGN.md)) and will want. Teaching the dev backend to tolerate them
72	would spend the one environment where such a rule could be developed. So compression runs
73	against the emulator, where a virtual clock is honest, and the dev project only ever sees
74	plausible traffic.
75	
76	Real-time mode against the dev project is what proves the backend works. Compressed mode
77	against the emulator is what makes time-dependent scenarios — presence going stale, a
78	cooldown expiring, a message that arrives one second too late — cheap enough to keep as
79	regression cases.
80	
81	## Sim time: the wire contract
82	
83	In compressed mode the console supplies the instant itself. Two fields carry it, both
84	namespaced under a single `sim` object so one predicate finds them:
85	
86	- on the `sendMessage` call: `sim.now` — the virtual instant the send happens at;
87	- on a presence write: `sim.updatedAt` — the virtual instant the heartbeat was reported
88	  at, standing in for `serverTimestamp()`.
89	
90	There is no third field and no bare top-level spelling. One object, one predicate, one
91	thing to strip.
92	
93	## Why sim fields cannot reach production
94	
95	A field that lets a client dictate the server's notion of *now* is the strongest
96	capability in this system: it defeats the cooldown, it revives stale presence, and it
97	backdates delivery. It exists because the emulator needs it, and four independent guards
98	keep it there. Each is meant to hold alone.
99	
100	1. **The server admits it only under the emulator.** The gate is a runtime signal a
101	   deployed function cannot carry (`FUNCTIONS_EMULATOR`, which the Functions emulator sets
102	   and a deploy never does) — read once at module load into a single exported constant, and
103	   never re-derived from anything in a request. A request cannot argue its way past it,
104	   because nothing in the request is consulted.
105	2. **The edge strips it.** Outside the emulator the callable deletes the `sim` object from
106	   the request before a single line of handler logic reads it, and logs that it did. The
107	   handler is therefore written against a request shape where the field cannot exist, and
108	   the log is what makes a stripped request distinguishable from one that never carried the
109	   field — a swallowed strip is a silent capability, which is what
110	   [basics](../.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/RULES.md) means by code that can silently do
111	   nothing.
112	3. **Firestore rules reject it.** Presence writes carrying a client-set `updatedAt` are
113	   refused by the ruleset, so the capability is closed at the boundary the functions do not
114	   sit in front of.
115	4. **No product client can send it.** The app under `app/` has no code that writes a `sim`
116	   field, and a committed check keeps it that way — the console is the only client that
117	   knows the spelling.
118	
119	Guards 1 and 2 are the server's; 3 is the boundary's; 4 is the client's. The
120	[spec-driven-product](../.claudinite/shared/packs/spec-driven-product/RULES.md) rule that
121	a requirement is proved at every tier that enforces it applies exactly here: this is one
122	requirement with four proofs, not one proof reused.
123	
124	## What the console observes
125	
126	Per actor: its live feed, its presence doc's freshness, and its position on the map. Per
127	send: the origin, the radius circle, the `recipientCount` the callable returned, and which
128	of the four actually received it — the matrix that makes a delivery bug visible rather
129	than inferable. A send whose reported count and observed recipients disagree is the
130	console's headline finding, because that disagreement is the one bug the app itself can
131	never show you.
132	
133	## Its executable requirements
134	
135	`dev/console/requirements/` — its own numbered spec, its own coverage gate, its own
136	gallery, in the shape [dev/requirements/](../dev/requirements/README.md) established. A
137	separate suite rather than new sections in the app's: the app's requirements document is
138	what the owner reads to approve *the product*, and an internal instrument's screens do not
139	belong in that review.
140

input.title: Console and secret setup for the dev console and the Appetize preview
input.body:
Everything under #379 that only a person can do, front-loaded so no later step waits on it.
Work top to bottom; the background is below the list.

- [ ] Confirm the project `shouts-whispers-dev` exists — [Firebase console](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/overview)
- [ ] Upgrade it to the Blaze plan — [Usage and billing](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/usage)
- [ ] Enable the Email/Password provider — [Sign-in method](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/providers)
- [ ] Add the user `sim1@shoutsandwhispers.test` with a password you keep — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Add `sim2@shoutsandwhispers.test` with the same password — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Add `sim3@shoutsandwhispers.test` with the same password — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Add `sim4@shoutsandwhispers.test` with the same password — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Add `demo@shoutsandwhispers.test` with a different password — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Post the two passwords to this issue, or say here where they are kept
- [ ] Enable Hosting on the project — [Hosting](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/hosting/sites)
- [ ] Press Generate new private key and keep the JSON file it downloads once — [Service accounts](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/settings/serviceaccounts/adminsdk)
- [ ] Paste that whole JSON as the secret `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` — [Repository secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers/settings/secrets/actions)
- [ ] Run `flutterfire configure` against the project from `app/`, and attach the generated `firebase_options.dart` and `google-services.json` to this issue
- [ ] Create an Appetize account — [appetize.io](https://appetize.io/)
- [ ] Copy the API token from the account page, where it is shown under API
- [ ] Paste it as the secret `APPETIZE_API_TOKEN` — [Repository secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers/settings/secrets/actions)

## Done when

Opening [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
lists five accounts, and
[Repository secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers/settings/secrets/actions)
lists both `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` and `APPETIZE_API_TOKEN`.

## Why each of these

**The project and Blaze.** Whether `shouts-whispers-dev` exists at all is unverified — the
session that planned #379 could not tell an absent project from a permission denial, and
`cloudfunctions.net` was egress-blocked. Cloud Functions need Blaze; without it the
backend cannot be deployed and neither half of #379 has anything to talk to.

**Email/password and the five accounts.** The app has only Google Sign-In today, which
uses Android Credential Manager and therefore Google Play services — which an Appetize
emulator device may not have. Email/password is the path that does not depend on it. Four
`sim*` accounts are what the console drives; `demo@` is what a visitor to the Appetize
preview signs in as. The four sims share a password because the console asks for one
password and signs in all four; `demo@` differs because its password ends up in the public
README.

**Where the passwords go.** The console is deployed publicly on the dev site, so its
bundle must not carry them — the operator types them once and the browser keeps them
(`docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md`). Nothing automated needs the sim passwords; they are for whoever
drives the console.

**Hosting.** How the console is reached. Without it, validating the console means having a
Flutter toolchain and a checkout, which was the option this plan chose against.

**`FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`.** What deploys functions, rules and the Hosting site from an
unattended run. Without it every deploy is a person at a terminal, and the chain's deploy
link parks.

**`flutterfire configure` output.** `app/lib/firebase_options.dart` is a committed
placeholder that throws; an APK built as-is opens on a setup screen. These files are what
the Android build link injects from secrets — they are attached here rather than committed
because `google-services.json` carries the project's real client config.

**`APPETIZE_API_TOKEN`.** What uploads the APK. Only the last link of #379 needs it, but
it is here because a secret created late is a chain that stops for a person late.

input.title: Sim-time wire contract and the four guards that keep it out of production
input.body:
Blocked-by: #380, #382
Model: opus
Automerge: under:firebase; under:.claudinite/local/packs/shouts-and-whispers

First link of the chain under #379. Read `docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md` on `main` before starting —
it is this link's specification, and if it is not there, #380's PR never merged: converge
as `action` naming that rather than inventing the contract.

## What to build

The `sim` wire fields described in that doc's "Sim time" and "Why sim fields cannot reach
production" sections, server-side only. No client writes them yet; this link is the
capability and its four guards, landing before anything can use it.

1. **The emulator gate.** One exported constant in `firebase/functions/src/`, read once at
   module load from the runtime signal, never re-derived per request. `FUNCTIONS_EMULATOR`
   is the candidate — **verify it empirically before depending on it**: run the Functions
   emulator, log the value, and record what you read in this issue. Do not take it from
   memory or from a comment; basics requires platform behaviour verified against a real run.
   If it turns out not to hold, find the signal that does and say so here.
2. **The edge strip.** In `sendMessage`, before any handler logic reads the request: when
   not under the emulator, delete `request.data.sim` and `logger.warn` that a sim field was
   stripped, naming the uid. The handler below it is written against a shape where the field
   cannot exist.
3. **Under the emulator**, `sim.now` replaces the callable's notion of now (cooldown
   comparison, message timestamp) and `sim.updatedAt` is accepted on a presence write in
   place of `serverTimestamp()`. Validate both like any boundary input — a finite number, a
   plausible range — and reject with `invalid-argument`, per the firebase pack.
4. **Firestore rules.** `firestore.rules` rejects a presence write carrying a client-set
   `updatedAt`. This holds whether or not the functions ran.
5. **A check in the local pack** asserting no file under `app/lib/` mentions the `sim`
   field spelling — the fourth guard, that no product client knows it. Write it per the
   writing-repo-scanning-checks skill, and watch it fail before you make it pass (introduce
   the string in a scratch copy, see red, remove it).

## Tests

Vitest, no emulator needed for the pure parts: the strip happens outside the emulator and
does not happen inside it; a `sim.now` outside the accepted range is rejected; the cooldown
is judged against `sim.now` under the emulator and against the server clock otherwise. The
rules change gets a rules test if the repo has a harness for one, and says plainly here if
it does not.

If a new constant is shared across tiers, it is a four-part change — the DESIGN.md §10 row,
`firebase/functions/src/constants.ts`, `app/lib/config.dart`, and the `PAIRS` map in the
`cross-tier-constants` check. A sim-only constant belongs to the server alone and stays out
of `PAIRS`.

## Done when

`cd firebase/functions && npm run build && npm test` is green, the local pack's
`node --test .claudinite/local/packs/shouts-and-whispers/pack.test.mjs` is green, and this
issue carries the emulator signal you actually observed.

input.title: Dev console package: plan model, plan editor, and its requirements suite
input.body:
Blocked-by: #383
Model: opus
Automerge: under:dev/console

Second link of the chain under #379. Start by reading `firebase/functions/src/` on `main`
for the sim-time constant #383 landed; if it is absent, that link's PR never merged —
converge as `action` naming it rather than building on air. (This link does not use the
field yet, but its absence means the chain is out of order.)

## What to build

`dev/console/` — a Flutter web package, and `dev/console/requirements/` — its own
executable-requirements suite, in the shape `dev/requirements/` established (its README is
the reference; copy the gate, the runner and the gallery tool, adapting paths).

This link is the console standing still: the plan document and the editor that produces it.
Nothing signs in, nothing writes to Firebase, nothing replays — that is #384's half.

- **The plan model**, pure Dart: four actors, each a list of timestamped waypoints and a
  list of sends (offset, kind, text); a plan duration; JSON round-trip.
- **Plausibility validation**: a waypoint pair implying a speed above a walking bound is
  rejected by the model, as is a per-actor send rate above the send cooldown. State both
  bounds as named constants in the console package — they are the console's own, not
  cross-tier, so they stay out of the `PAIRS` map.
- **The editor**: a `flutter_map` view with the four actors' paths, placing and dragging
  waypoints, placing sends along a path, and a per-actor lane showing its sends in time
  order.
- **Geohash reuse**: depend on `app/`'s `lib/geo/geohash.dart` by path rather than copying
  it. A third transcription of that encoder is exactly what `docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md` chose
  Flutter to avoid.

## Its spec

Doc-first: write the leaves in `dev/console/requirements/requirements.md` and watch the
coverage gate go red before writing the cases. Use the same kinds — `screen` for a resting
state, `saga` for placing a path and a send, `behavior` for a driven gesture, `logic` for
the plausibility rules. Propose the goldens for these brand-new leaves; never regenerate a
committed one to turn a case green.

Confirm as you go that two requirements suites coexist in this repo — the
executable-requirements pack activates on `dev/requirements/requirements.md`, and if its
checks assume exactly one suite, say so in this issue rather than working around it.

## Done when

`cd dev/console && flutter analyze` is at zero issues and
`cd dev/console/requirements && flutter test` is green, with the gallery gate current.

input.title: Console replay engine and observation views, real-time against dev
input.body:
Blocked-by: #384
Model: opus
Automerge: under:dev/console

Third link of the chain under #379. Start by reading `dev/console/` on `main` for the plan
model and editor #384 landed; if the package is absent, converge as `action` naming that
link rather than rebuilding it.

## What to build

The console at 1×, against the real dev project — the half that makes it an instrument
rather than a drawing tool.

- **Four signed-in actors.** Four named `FirebaseApp` instances, each signed in with
  email/password as one `sim*@shoutsandwhispers.test` account, each with its own Firestore
  client and its own feed subscription. Passwords are typed by the operator into the
  console and kept in browser storage — never in the bundle, never committed
  (`docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md`, "Credentials"). #382 carries the accounts and their password.
- **The player.** Replays a plan at 1× against wall-clock time: interpolates each actor's

input.title: Validation gate: drive the dev console and confirm it works
input.body:
The gate under #379: nothing in the Appetize half starts until this issue closes. Open the
console URL #388 posted, with the sim passwords from #382 to hand.

- [ ] Sign the four sim actors in
- [ ] Draw a path for two of them that crosses within 150 m
- [ ] Place a whisper on the first actor at the crossing point
- [ ] Place a shout on the first actor while the second is 500 m away
- [ ] Press play and watch the run to the end
- [ ] Read the whisper's reported recipient count against who actually received it
- [ ] Read the shout's reported recipient count against who actually received it
- [ ] Switch to emulator mode and replay the same plan at 60×
- [ ] Comment here on anything that looked wrong, then close this issue

## What you are looking for

The whisper should reach the second actor and the shout should not — the shout reaches
1,500 m, so it should reach *both*, and the whisper only the one inside 150 m. If the
counts and the observed recipients disagree, that is the bug this whole instrument was
built to make visible; comment it rather than closing, and it becomes its own issue.

The 60× replay is checking a different thing: that compressed mode runs against the emulator
and never against dev. If the speed control is available while the console is pointed at the
dev project, that is a guard failure and the gate does not pass.

## What closing this releases

The Appetize chain: the app's email/password sign-in path, the Android build wiring, the
upload, and the public preview link. All of it is written and queued behind this issue, so
closing it is the only action needed to start it.

Leaving it open costs nothing — the console is already deployed and usable, and the queue
simply waits.

input.title: Email/password sign-in path in the app
input.body:
Blocked-by: #389
Model: opus
Automerge: under:app; under:dev/requirements

First link of the Appetize half of #379, released by the validation gate. Read #389's
closing comment first: if it closed with the console judged broken, that is not a release —
converge as `action` and say so.

## Why the app needs this at all

`FirebaseAuthAdapter` offers only Google Sign-In, which in `google_sign_in` v7 goes through
Android Credential Manager and therefore Google Play services. An Appetize emulator device
may not carry Play services, and the sign-in would fail in a way the plugin reports as a
user cancellation (its own README says configuration errors surface as `canceled`). Nothing
about the preview works if the visitor cannot sign in, so the preview needs a path that does
not depend on Play services at all.

## What to build

An email/password sign-in on `AuthPort` beside `signInWithGoogle`, implemented in
`FirebaseAuthAdapter` with `signInWithEmailAndPassword`, and a sign-in screen that offers
both. Errors map to the port's existing `SignInException` shape rather than leaking
`FirebaseAuthException` into the UI — the ports boundary is the flutter pack's rule and an
import-scan test enforces it.

This is a product change, not a demo flag: it ships in the app for everyone. Decide
deliberately whether the second path is always visible or only when the account exists, and
say which you chose and why in this issue.

## Its spec

New leaves in `dev/requirements/requirements.md` — doc-first, red before green: the sign-in
screen's resting state with both options, and the driven behavior of an email sign-in
reaching the port. Propose the new goldens; the sign-in screen's existing golden will move,
and a moved golden is an owner decision — surface actual, expected and diff in this issue
and ask before re-baselining it.

green, and the moved golden has been approved in this issue rather than quietly regenerated.

input.title: Android build wiring and the Appetize preview workflow
input.body:

on `main` for the email/password path #390 landed; absent means that link never merged —

## What stands in the way today

- `app/lib/firebase_options.dart` is a committed placeholder that throws; `main.dart` catches
  it and shows the setup screen. An APK built as-is opens on that screen.
- The **google-services Gradle plugin is not applied** — neither
  `app/android/settings.gradle.kts` nor `app/android/app/build.gradle.kts` mentions
  `com.google.gms.google-services`. Firebase Auth would initialize from
  `firebase_options.dart` regardless, but `google_sign_in` reads its web OAuth client from a
  Gradle-processed `google-services.json`, so the existing Google path breaks without it.
- No Android SDK is available to a queue run's sandbox; the APK is built on a GitHub runner,
  which carries one.

## What to build

1. Apply the google-services plugin in `app/android/`, keeping the application id as it is
   (`com.shoutsandwhispers.shouts_and_whispers` — a decision recorded on #379).
2. `.github/workflows/appetize-preview.yml`, `workflow_dispatch`: materialize
   `firebase_options.dart` and `google-services.json` from secrets, `flutter build apk
   --debug`, upload to Appetize with `APPETIZE_API_TOKEN`, and print the returned public key
   and URL in the job summary. Neither config file is ever committed
   (`docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md`).
3. Take the upload's request shape from Appetize's own current documentation at build time,
   not from #99's snippet — that snippet is unverified, written from an egress-blocked
   session, and their API has more than one version.

Same reasoning as #387 for why this is a workflow rather than a Claudinite task: the
vendored executor passes no repository secrets to a run.

`app/lib/firebase_options.dart` stays the committed throwing placeholder. The workflow
replaces it in the runner's checkout only — a build that silently fell back to the
placeholder must fail, so assert the file was written before building.

input.title: Confirm the Appetize preview is usable end to end
input.body:
The last human step of #379, and what closes #99's acceptance criteria. Open the preview URL
#392 posted.

- [ ] Launch the preview and wait for the app to boot past the splash
- [ ] Sign in as `demo@shoutsandwhispers.test`
- [ ] Confirm the map shows a position rather than a location error
- [ ] Send a whisper
- [ ] Confirm the sent message appears in your own feed
- [ ] Confirm the delivered-count snackbar names a number
- [ ] Comment what you saw, then close this issue

## Why a person does this

Everything up to here is readable by a machine: the workflow's conclusion, the page
responding, the README on `main`. Whether a Flutter app *behaves* on an emulated device in a
browser is not — it needs eyes on a session, and the two ways it plausibly fails are both
invisible to a URL fetch.

The first is sign-in. The demo path exists because Google Sign-In needs Play services the
Appetize device may lack; if the email/password path fails too, the finding belongs on #390.

The second is location. The app needs a GPS fix before it will send, so the preview must be
launched with a location injected. If the map shows a location error, the launch parameters
are wrong rather than the app — that is #392's to fix.

An empty feed with a working send is not a failure: with no sim actors running nearby, you
are your own only recipient, and your own copy arriving is the delivery contract working
(`docs/DESIGN.md` §1.5).

input.title: Retrospective: the dev console and the Appetize preview, one week on
input.body:
Blocked-by: #393
Not-before: 2026-10-05T09:00:00Z
Model: opus

The last link of the chain under #379. Its brief was written at design time, while the
expectations were still in front of someone; read `docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md` and #379 for what
the design meant to achieve, then answer the four questions from the real record.

## What was expected, in amounts

- **The console is used to answer a question about the backend at least once a week.** Zero
  runs in a week is the finding that matters most: it would mean the instrument was built
  and abandoned, and the four sim seats cost more than a seeder script would have.
- **At least one delivery bug is found through it** in the first month. The console exists
  because a reported `recipientCount` disagreeing with observed recipients is invisible from
  the app. If nothing was ever found, either the backend is correct (good, and worth saying)
  or nobody looked.
- **Compressed mode is used for the time-dependent scenarios**, not just as a faster way to
  watch the same plan. Count the runs by mode.
- **The Appetize preview is opened by someone outside this repository.** If the link was
  never shared, the preview is a cost with no return and should be retired rather than
  maintained.
- **Zero `sim` fields stripped at the edge in production.** Guard 2 logs every strip; a
  non-zero count means a client is sending them and one of the four guards has already been
  the only thing standing.

## The four questions

1. **Is it working?** Read the console's real use, the deploy workflow's run history, and
   the strip log. Count parks and failed dispatches in this chain, not just the happy path.
2. **Is it misused?** Did anyone point the console at something it was not for — a
   long-running actor left replaying, a plan used as a load test?
3. **Is it overused?** Which parts cost attention and returned nothing? The four seats, the
   separate requirements suite and the emulator mode are each defensible and each cost real
   work; say which earned it.
4. **Is it underused?** What did the design mean to cover that nothing reaches? The
   time-dependent scenarios are the likeliest answer — they were the reason for the whole
   emulator half.

## How it ends

Comment the answers on #379, then close this issue as completed. A question you cannot read
an answer for is reported as unreadable, never estimated.

input.body:
Tracking issue for two initiatives run as one chain: a **dev console** that drives four
simulated accounts against the real backend, and — gated on a human validation of that
console — the **Appetize preview** of the Android app (#99).

The end state of the console, and why it is shaped this way, is `docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md`
(#380). This issue holds the plan; it is append-only from here.

## Why the console comes first

Nothing in this repository has ever observed the backend working. `app/`'s 21 tests and
`dev/requirements/`'s 70 cases all run against scripted fakes; the functions' 14 tests are
pure-logic. Hyperlocal delivery cannot be observed with one client — the product *is* who
else was near you — so the first real proof of the backend needs several clients at once.
That instrument is worth more than a demo link, and the demo link is better once it exists.

## Decisions taken (2026-09-06)

| decision | choice |
|---|---|
| demo/console backend | reuse `shouts-whispers-dev` |
| preview sign-in | email/password demo account (the app has only Google Sign-In today) |
| seeding | scripted sim actors from the console, not a static seeder |
| console stack | Flutter web, `dev/console/` |
| console spec | its own suite, `dev/console/requirements/` |
| console access | Firebase Hosting on the dev project |
| time control | real-time against dev; compressed against the emulator |
| Android app id | keep `com.shoutsandwhispers.shouts_and_whispers` |

## The plan

Phase 0 — out-of-band setup, human, front-loaded.

- [ ] #382 — Firebase console steps, five accounts, Hosting, and the two repository secrets

Phase 1 — the stack, merged as a chain, each link blocked behind the last.

- [ ] #380 — the design doc
- [ ] #383 — sim-time wire contract and its four guards: server, rules, checks
- [ ] #384 — console package, plan model, plan editor, and its requirements suite
- [ ] #385 — replay engine and observation views, real-time against dev
- [ ] #386 — compressed mode against the emulator suite
- [ ] #387 — the dev deploy workflow and Hosting config

Phase 2 — execution.

- [ ] #388 — dispatch the deploy, confirm the console serves, post its URL
- [ ] #389 — human validation gate. Nothing below starts until this closes.

Phase 3 — the Appetize preview (#99), released by that gate.

- [ ] #390 — email/password sign-in path in the app, with its requirement leaves
- [ ] #391 — google-services Gradle plugin and the Appetize build workflow
- [ ] #392 — dispatch the build, upload, capture the URL, document it
- [ ] #393 — human confirmation that the preview is usable end to end
- [ ] #394 — retrospective, held until 2026-10-05

## Expected human gates

Three: the phase-0 checklist (#382), the console validation gate (#389), and the preview
confirmation (#393). Every other link carries an automerge policy predicting its own folder,
so a park anywhere else means a change reached further than this plan predicted — which is
the speed bump working, not an error to route around.

## Two deviations from the corpus, recorded deliberately

**Workflows rather than Claudinite tasks** for the two deploy paths (#387, #391), against
claudinite-growth's rule preferring a task. The vendored executor passes exactly one secret
to a run (`CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN`), so no queue run can reach `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` or
`APPETIZE_API_TOKEN`. A dispatchable workflow is the only mechanism in this repository that
can; the chain's execution links dispatch it and read its conclusion, which they *can* do.

**The console's `sim` capability is a legacy-tolerance-shaped risk that is not scaffolding.**
It is permanent — the emulator mode needs it for as long as the console exists — so it ships
with four independent guards instead of a removal date. #394's retrospective reads the strip
log to check that none of them has been load-bearing.

## What was measured before planning (2026-09-06)

- `cd app && flutter test` — 21 passed
- `cd dev/requirements && python3 run_requirements.py` — 70 passed
- `cd firebase/functions && npm run build && npm test` — clean, 14 passed
- `node --test .claudinite/local/packs/shouts-and-whispers/pack.test.mjs` — 24 passed
- Whether `shouts-whispers-dev` exists and is deployed: **unverified**. Firestore's REST
  API answers `403 CONSUMER_INVALID` identically for a project that does not exist, and
  `cloudfunctions.net` is egress-blocked from the session that planned this. #382's first
  checkbox settles it.

input.body:
Planned as the second half of #379, behind a dev console that drives four scripted sim accounts against the real backend.

Three of this issue's open questions are now answered there: the demo talks to `shouts-whispers-dev` (reused, not a separate project); Android only for now; and the unmoderated-demo risk is accepted on the dev project, stated in the README the upload link writes.

Two of its assumptions turned out to need changing:

- **Sign-in.** `google_sign_in` v7 goes through Android Credential Manager, which needs Google Play services — which an Appetize emulator device may not carry, and whose absence the plugin reports as a user cancellation rather than a configuration error. The preview gets an email/password path in the app instead (#390).
- **Seeding.** A static seed decays: `PRESENCE_TTL_MS` is five minutes, so seeded presence is stale before most visitors arrive. Live scripted actors from the console replace it.

Also worth recording against step 3 of the plan here: the `curl` snippet in this issue is unverified — `docs.appetize.io` is egress-blocked from the sessions that can plan this, and Appetize has more than one API version. #392 takes the request shape from their live docs at build time rather than from that snippet.

The work is filed and queued: #382 is the human setup, and everything through #394 runs behind it.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.
