1	# The dev console — scripted actors against the real backend
2	
3	The app's executable requirements ([dev/requirements/](../dev/requirements/requirements.md))
4	prove every screen and gesture against scripted fakes: no phone, no server, no
5	network. Nothing in this repository exercises the other half — that a real client,
6	holding a real token, writing real presence, gets the delivery
7	[DESIGN.md §4](DESIGN.md) describes. Hyperlocal delivery cannot be observed with one
8	client: the whole product is *who else was near you*, and a single device is always
9	alone in its cell.
10	
11	The dev console is that second half. It is a second client of the same backend, driving
12	four simulated accounts along planned paths, sending planned messages, and showing what
13	each of the four actually received.
14	
15	## What it is
16	
17	A Flutter web app at `dev/console/`, deployed to Firebase Hosting on the dev project. It
18	is a development instrument, not part of the product: it ships in no store, it is never
19	pointed at production, and the app under `app/` neither imports it nor knows it exists.
20	
21	It is Flutter for one reason that outweighs the rest: it reuses this repository's
22	committed geohash encoder (`app/lib/geo/geohash.dart`) and message models by path
23	dependency rather than transcribing them a third time. A TypeScript console would add a
24	third copy of the encoding contract the
25	[shouts-and-whispers pack](../.claudinite/local/packs/shouts-and-whispers/RULES.md)
26	already spends two checks guarding, and would need a parallel requirements harness built
27	from nothing.
28	
29	## The four actors
30	
31	Four email/password accounts on the dev project, signed in simultaneously through four
32	named `FirebaseApp` instances so each holds its own auth state, its own Firestore client
33	and its own feed subscription. The backend sees four ordinary users; nothing about a sim
34	actor is privileged, and the console holds no admin credential.
35	
36	Four, rather than a number, because four is what the interesting cases need: a sender, a
37	recipient inside the whisper radius, a recipient inside the shout radius but outside the
38	whisper's, and one who is out of range or stale. Every delivery rule in
39	[DESIGN.md §1](DESIGN.md) is expressible with those four seats.
40	
41	## The plan
42	
43	A plan is the console's document, and it is pure data — editable, replayable, and
44	shareable as JSON:
45	
46	- **A path per actor**: waypoints on the map with a time offset each. Between two
47	  waypoints the actor moves at whatever speed the pair implies; the editor rejects a pair
48	  implying a speed no person walks.
49	- **Sends pinned along the path**: an offset, a kind (shout or whisper), and the text.
50	  The send happens wherever the actor is at that offset, and the console draws the
51	  message's origin and its radius on the map.
52	- **A duration** the plan runs for.
53	
54	The editor is the product surface: place a path, place a send, press play, watch the four
55	feeds fill.
56	
57	## Two run modes, and why the fast one cannot use the real backend
58	
59	| | real-time | compressed |
60	|---|---|---|
61	| speed | 1× | any multiplier |
62	| backend | the dev project | the Firebase emulator suite |
63	| clock | Firestore `serverTimestamp()` | a virtual clock the console supplies |
64	| what it proves | the real fan-out, rules and callable work end to end | the delivery rules hold across time-dependent scenarios |
65	
66	Compressed replay cannot run against a real backend, and not merely because
67	`PRESENCE_TTL_MS` is judged server-side against a clock no client can move. A plan
68	replayed at 60× *is* an actor walking at 600 km/h and sending twenty messages a second.
69	Those are exactly the shapes a real backend should learn to refuse — implausible speed and
70	implausible rate are anti-spoofing signals the product does not have yet
71	([DESIGN.md §7](DESIGN.md)) and will want. Teaching the dev backend to tolerate them
72	would spend the one environment where such a rule could be developed. So compression runs
73	against the emulator, where a virtual clock is honest, and the dev project only ever sees
74	plausible traffic.
75	
76	Real-time mode against the dev project is what proves the backend works. Compressed mode
77	against the emulator is what makes time-dependent scenarios — presence going stale, a
78	cooldown expiring, a message that arrives one second too late — cheap enough to keep as
79	regression cases.
80	
81	## Sim time: the wire contract
82	
83	In compressed mode the console supplies the instant itself. Two fields carry it, both
84	namespaced under a single `sim` object so one predicate finds them:
85	
86	- on the `sendMessage` call: `sim.now` — the virtual instant the send happens at;
87	- on a presence write: `sim.updatedAt` — the virtual instant the heartbeat was reported
88	  at, standing in for `serverTimestamp()`.
89	
90	There is no third field and no bare top-level spelling. One object, one predicate, one
91	thing to strip.
92	
93	## Why sim fields cannot reach production
94	
95	A field that lets a client dictate the server's notion of *now* is the strongest
96	capability in this system: it defeats the cooldown, it revives stale presence, and it
97	backdates delivery. It exists because the emulator needs it, and four independent guards
98	keep it there. Each is meant to hold alone.
99	
100	1. **The server admits it only under the emulator.** The gate is a runtime signal a
101	   deployed function cannot carry (`FUNCTIONS_EMULATOR`, which the Functions emulator sets
102	   and a deploy never does) — read once at module load into a single exported constant, and
103	   never re-derived from anything in a request. A request cannot argue its way past it,
104	   because nothing in the request is consulted.
105	2. **The edge strips it.** Outside the emulator the callable deletes the `sim` object from
106	   the request before a single line of handler logic reads it, and logs that it did. The
107	   handler is therefore written against a request shape where the field cannot exist, and
108	   the log is what makes a stripped request distinguishable from one that never carried the
109	   field — a swallowed strip is a silent capability, which is what
110	   [basics](../.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/RULES.md) means by code that can silently do
111	   nothing.
112	3. **Firestore rules reject it.** Presence writes carrying a client-set `updatedAt` are
113	   refused by the ruleset, so the capability is closed at the boundary the functions do not
114	   sit in front of.
115	4. **No product client can send it.** The app under `app/` has no code that writes a `sim`
116	   field, and a committed check keeps it that way — the console is the only client that
117	   knows the spelling.
118	
119	Guards 1 and 2 are the server's; 3 is the boundary's; 4 is the client's. The
120	[spec-driven-product](../.claudinite/shared/packs/spec-driven-product/RULES.md) rule that
121	a requirement is proved at every tier that enforces it applies exactly here: this is one
122	requirement with four proofs, not one proof reused.
123	
124	## What the console observes
125	
126	Per actor: its live feed, its presence doc's freshness, and its position on the map. Per
127	send: the origin, the radius circle, the `recipientCount` the callable returned, and which
128	of the four actually received it — the matrix that makes a delivery bug visible rather
129	than inferable. A send whose reported count and observed recipients disagree is the
130	console's headline finding, because that disagreement is the one bug the app itself can
131	never show you.
132	
133	## Its executable requirements
134	
135	`dev/console/requirements/` — its own numbered spec, its own coverage gate, its own
136	gallery, in the shape [dev/requirements/](../dev/requirements/README.md) established. A
137	separate suite rather than new sections in the app's: the app's requirements document is
138	what the owner reads to approve *the product*, and an internal instrument's screens do not
139	belong in that review.
140

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- create-release-plan: The Firebase release standard — two separate dev/prod projects with the committed default pinned to dev, prod config injected only by the release pipeline, App Check attestation gating, and deliberate promotion. Use when planning a Firebase-backed app's first release, splitting a project into dev and prod, wiring prod config and App Check into a release pipeline, or editing firebase.json or .firebaserc.
- deterministic-expecteds: What makes a rendered expected byte-stable — the pinned clock, faked inputs, real fonts, fixed-duration pumps — and the per-stack rendering recipe (jsdom+satori for DOM products, Flutter golden files) with pixel-exact comparison. Use when writing a case, the render harness or the fake world under dev/requirements.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- firebase-functions: Writing Cloud Functions for Firebase — transactional rate limits, batched-write chunking and at-least-once fan-out, best-effort push with dead-token cleanup, smoke-loading the built entrypoint. Use when editing anything under functions/.
- firestore-security-rules: Writing and testing Firestore and Storage security rules — default-deny, merge semantics, absent-field guards, server-owned fields, request.time pins, bounded strings, empirical rules tests. Use when editing firestore.rules or storage.rules, or reviewing what a ruleset allows.
- flutter-golden-tests: Widget-test and golden mechanics in Flutter — loading real fonts before a golden, fixed-duration pumps instead of pumpAndSettle around spinners, one fixed viewport per suite. Use when writing or debugging a widget test or golden, or when goldens render as boxes, hang, or drift.
- flutter-pubspec: Telling a real dependency change from lockfile churn in a Flutter app — a pubspec.lock that moved without pubspec.yaml is SDK version skew to revert, not a change to commit. Use when pubspec.lock shows up in a diff, or when editing pubspec.yaml or pubspec.lock.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- node-test-discovery: Wiring a `node --test` invocation so it finds the suite — dot-directories are skipped, a path that matches nothing runs zero tests and exits green. Loaded for any edit of a workflow or package.json test script.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- write-a-requirement-leaf: How a requirement leaf is written in the executable spec — the backtick-numbered one-liner with its detail collapsed under it, and which kind (surface snapshot, behavior, logic, saga, per-project, e2e singleton) its case takes. Use when adding or reshaping a requirement line in requirements.md.
- write-a-saga: How a saga case is written — a multi-step story captured as a golden storyboard or one animated APNG golden — steps, captions, frame budget, the real entry point, delay stripping and gesture marking. Use when authoring or changing a case under the saga kind.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it
   again. (1)
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.
